patch.objective: Apply consent, refusal and capacity in the field
secondaryObjectives: Analyze cues to choose among competing hypotheses in a patient with altered mental status
Work within medical direction, protocols and the limits of AEMT scope

sources.cite: National Registry of EMTs. AEMT examination test plan
sources.note: Relayed from the course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/ems.ts and labs/ems-sources.ts, read in NREMT's own documents 2026-11-09); not re-read for this case. EMS Operations: consent, refusal and capacity in the field.

sources.cite: NASEMSO. National Model EMS Clinical Guidelines, Version 3.0 (March 2022): Patient Refusals
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the full text Iowa HHS hosts (https://hhs.iowa.gov/media/198/download) through summarizing fetches with quotes; NASEMSO's own page, read the same day, still presents Version 3 (2022) as current and names no later version. Capacity: 'alert, oriented, and can understand the circumstances surrounding his/her illness or impairment', judgment not significantly impaired by illness, injury or intoxication; a patient without capacity 'should not be allowed to refuse care against medical advice or to be released at the scene'; explain 'the possible risks and overall concerns'; doubts about capacity: contact medical direction; document the plan, who will be with the patient, and the patient's own words; tell them they may call again.

sources.cite: NASEMSO. National Model EMS Clinical Guidelines, Version 3.0 (March 2022): Hypoglycemia
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the full text Iowa HHS hosts (https://hhs.iowa.gov/media/198/download) through summarizing fetches with quotes; NASEMSO's own page, read the same day, still presents Version 3 (2022) as current and names no later version. Treat at 60 mg/dL or less; oral glucose for a conscious patient with a patent airway (adult 25 g); release without transport only if all are true: repeat glucose above 80 mg/dL, takes insulin or metformin and 'does not take long-acting oral sulphunylurea agents', normal mental status with no focal signs, can promptly eat a carbohydrate meal, and 'a reliable adult will be staying with patient'. Altered Mental Status: a glucose check is part of the assessment.

sources.cite: American Diabetes Association. Hypoglycemia Guidelines: your visual guide to the guidelines (infographic based on the Standards of Care in Diabetes, 2025)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes: level 1 below 70 mg/dL, level 2 below 54 mg/dL, level 3 'Altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance, irrespective of glucose level'; 'In most conscious individuals, have 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrates, and recheck glucose in 15 minutes', repeated until it resolves; 'Glucagon is indicated for hypoglycemia treatment when people are unable or unwilling to consume carbohydrates by mouth'; ready-to-use glucagon can be given by people who are not health care professionals. The page says nothing about exercise.

sources.cite: NHTSA. National EMS Scope of Practice Model 2019: Including Change Notices 1.0 and 2.0 (DOT HS 813 151, 2021-08-01)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17: the record page (title, report number, date; the change notices add intramuscular injection, vaccination in a public health emergency and nasal swab collection at EMT and above) and the PDF's skill tables through a summarizing fetch whose table columns were partly unclear, so placement was checked against the course's own reading (backend/supabase/seed/labs/ems-sources.ts, 2026-11-09) and REQ-241's reading (2026-11-11). EMR: oxygen, BVM, naloxone (intranasal or auto-injector), unit-dose hazmat antidote auto-injectors, tourniquet, wound packing, emergency moves, manual stabilization; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, oral glucose, aspirin, the patient's own nitroglycerin, an inhaled bronchodilator, CPAP, the epinephrine auto-injector. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways, waveform capnography, sublingual nitroglycerin and a limited list of IV and IM drugs (dextrose, naloxone). Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing, needle chest decompression, intubation and medicated infusions. No newer model was found on 2026-11-17.

His glucose (46 mg/dL) and its rise after one tube of oral glucose (to about 110 mg/dL over 15 minutes) are authored; so is the rule that he agrees to go only once the specific risk of his sulfonylurea is explained and the physician on medical direction speaks to him, and that a plain release leads to a second low three hours later. FLAG: no source gives these timings. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

brief.situation: 07:50. You are an AEMT on an ambulance with an EMT partner. Joan called because her husband Gary, 66, was sweaty and confused at breakfast. He has type 2 diabetes. He is in a kitchen chair, telling you to leave.
handover: Joan has his medication bag: glipizide and metformin.
Within AEMT scope: glucose monitoring, oral glucose for a patient who can swallow (IV dextrose is for one who cannot), transport, and a refusal process with medical direction.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Every assessment and treatment takes the time it would on a real call. Scene time and the drive run on the clock.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends when care is handed over, then a debrief scores what you did.
